Jesse Michael (Principal Security Researcher, Eclypsium) presents practical techniques for achieving persistent code execution below the operating system through UEFI firmware exploitation.

UEFI Attack Surface

The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface runs before any OS code and has access to all hardware. Vulnerabilities in UEFI DXE drivers — which receive minimal security review — allow writing persistent code to SPI flash that survives OS reinstalls and disk replacements.

Secure Boot Bypass Techniques

The talk demonstrates techniques for bypassing UEFI Secure Boot: exploiting signed-but-vulnerable UEFI drivers (BootHole predecessors), abusing the OptionROM loading mechanism, and leveraging vendor-specific maintenance modes that disable signature verification.

Implant Capabilities

A UEFI implant can modify the OS bootloader, inject malicious kernel modules, and establish persistence that cannot be detected or removed by any OS-level security tool — only firmware re-flashing eliminates the implant.

talks.title: Jens Muller - Covert Attacks on Email End-to-End Encryption
talks.teaser: Extends EFAIL research with new covert channel attacks that exfiltrate PGP and S/MIME plaintext without triggering known detection mechanisms.
talks.summary:
Covert Email Encryption Attacks

Jens Muller (PhD researcher, Ruhr University Bochum) presents new attacks against email end-to-end encryption, extending the EFAIL research with novel covert channel exfiltration techniques.

EFAIL Recap

The EFAIL vulnerabilities (CVE-2017-17688, CVE-2017-17689) demonstrated that many email clients decrypt PGP/S-MIME messages in an HTML rendering context, allowing adversaries who intercept encrypted emails to craft malicious wrappers that exfiltrate plaintext via CSS background image URLs or HTML form submissions when the victim's client opens the email.

New Covert Channels

Muller identifies additional exfiltration channels not addressed by EFAIL patches: DNS-based exfiltration through MX record lookups triggered during email rendering, and HTTP/2 server push covert channels in email clients with embedded browser renderers.

Mitigation and Detection Gaps

Existing mitigations (disabling remote content loading) fail to address DNS-based channels. The talk provides complete detection guidance and advocates for email client architectural changes that isolate decryption from rendering.

talks.title: Jeff Dileo - Evil eBPF: Practical Abuses of In-Kernel Bytecode Runtime
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how eBPF programs can be weaponized to create undetectable Linux kernel rootkits with full privilege and persistent covert channels.
talks.summary:
eBPF as an Offensive Primitive

Jeff Dileo presents research on abusing the Linux eBPF subsystem — a technology designed for safe kernel instrumentation — as an offensive capability for rootkits, privilege escalation, and detection evasion.

eBPF Background

Extended Berkeley Packet Filter allows loading small, sandboxed programs into the Linux kernel via the bpf() syscall, with the kernel verifier ensuring memory safety. eBPF is widely deployed for observability (perf, bcc), networking (XDP, TC), and security (Falco, Seccomp).

Weaponizing eBPF

Dileo demonstrates loading eBPF programs that hook system calls (via kprobe/tracepoint attachments) to intercept and modify kernel operations without modifiable kernel code — creating a rootkit that hides files, network connections, and processes from standard Linux observation tools while evading loadable kernel module detection.

Privilege Escalation

eBPF programs loaded with CAP_BPF (available in Linux 5.8+) can read arbitrary kernel memory and overwrite cred structures to escalate to root, bypassing traditional SUID binary requirements.

talks.title: Jayson Grace - MOSE: Using Configuration Management for Evil
talks.teaser: Introduces MOSE, an open-source tool for weaponizing Chef, Puppet, Ansible, and Salt configuration management systems during red team engagements.
talks.summary:
Weaponizing Configuration Management

Jayson Grace presents MOSE (Master of Server Exploitation), an open-source offensive tool designed to weaponize enterprise configuration management systems during red team engagements.

Configuration Management Attack Surface

Chef, Puppet, Ansible, and Salt are deployed to manage configuration across thousands of servers simultaneously — making the configuration management infrastructure one of the highest-value lateral movement targets in enterprise networks.

MOSE Architecture

MOSE automates the process of identifying the configuration management system in use, locating the orchestration server, and injecting malicious code into the management system's configuration manifests. On the next agent run, the malicious code executes on all managed nodes.

Real-World Attack Scenarios

Grace demonstrates deploying a Cobalt Strike beacon to 3,000+ servers simultaneously through a compromised Chef server, achieving complete environment compromise from a single pivot point with no additional lateral movement required.

talks.title: Jatin Kataria - 100 Seconds of Solitude: Defeating Cisco Trust Anchor
talks.teaser: Demonstrates a practical bypass of Cisco Trust Anchor Module (TAm), breaking hardware-rooted secure boot on enterprise routers.
talks.summary:
Bypassing Cisco Trust Anchor

Jatin Kataria (Principal Security Researcher, Red Balloon Security) presents research demonstrating a practical bypass of the Cisco Trust Anchor Module (TAm), Cisco's hardware root of trust implemented in a dedicated FPGA on enterprise routers and switches.

Cisco Trust Anchor Architecture

The Trust Anchor Module is an FPGA that performs cryptographic verification of the Cisco IOS image before boot, establishing a hardware root of trust that Cisco claims makes it impossible to run unauthorized firmware even with physical access.

The Attack: FPGA Bitstream Manipulation

Kataria demonstrates that the TAm FPGA bitstream, stored in SPI flash, can be extracted and analyzed. By identifying and patching the specific bitstream logic that performs the cryptographic signature verification, the TAm can be made to approve any firmware image — defeating the hardware root of trust entirely.

Impact and Remediation

The attack affects all Cisco devices with TAm across multiple product lines (ISR, ASR, CSR, NCS series). Remediation requires physical hardware replacement as the vulnerability is in the FPGA bitstream provisioning process.

talks.title: Jacob Baines - Help Me Vulnerabilities, You're My Only Hope
talks.teaser: Presents a practical exploitation guide for finding and exploiting memory corruption vulnerabilities in network security devices and embedded Linux systems.
talks.summary:
Exploiting Network Security Appliances

Jacob Baines (Vulnerability Researcher, Tenable) presents a practical guide to finding and exploiting memory corruption vulnerabilities in network security appliances — routers, firewalls, VPN concentrators, and UTM devices.

Attack Surface Overview

Network security appliances run stripped-down embedded Linux with minimal exploit mitigations (often no ASLR, NX, or stack canaries due to legacy toolchains), exposed attack surface through management web interfaces, and privileged network positions.

Vulnerability Discovery Methodology

Baines presents a structured approach: firmware extraction (UART/JTAG/download), static analysis with Ghidra to identify dangerous function calls (strcpy, sprintf in HTTP handlers), and targeted fuzzing using AFL with custom network protocol mutators.

Heap Exploitation Techniques

The talk covers heap exploitation techniques adapted for embedded Linux environments — glibc heap internals at 2.27, fastbin attacks, and tcache poisoning — applied to real CVEs in Fortinet and Cisco management interfaces.

talks.title: Jack Baker - Hacking WebAssembly Games with Binary Instrumentation
talks.teaser: Demonstrates memory editing and cheat development for WebAssembly-based browser games using dynamic binary instrumentation.
talks.summary:
WebAssembly Game Hacking

Jack Baker presents techniques for hacking browser games compiled to WebAssembly, applying traditional binary game hacking methodologies to the web context.

WebAssembly Reverse Engineering

Wasm binaries use a compact binary format that can be disassembled into WAT (WebAssembly Text Format) and analyzed with tools like WABT and Ghidra's Wasm support. Baker demonstrates decompiling Wasm modules to identify game state variables and logic functions.

Memory Editing via JavaScript

WebAssembly modules share a linear memory buffer (WebAssembly.Memory) accessible from JavaScript. Baker demonstrates reading and writing game state (health, ammo, position, score) directly from the browser console by locating the relevant memory offsets through pattern scanning.

Binary Instrumentation Approach

For games with obfuscated Wasm or runtime-generated code, Baker uses Chrome DevTools Protocol-based instrumentation to hook Wasm function calls at the JavaScript/Wasm boundary, providing a dynamic analysis capability without modifying the Wasm binary.

talks.title: Itzik Kotler - Process Injection Techniques: Gotta Catch Them All
talks.teaser: Comprehensive catalog of 15+ Windows process injection techniques with detection signatures and evasion analysis for each.
talks.summary:
Windows Process Injection Taxonomy

Itzik Kotler (CTO and co-founder, SafeBreach) presents a comprehensive taxonomy of Windows process injection techniques, providing detection guidance and evasion analysis for each.

Taxonomy Coverage

The talk covers 15+ techniques: DLL injection, reflective DLL injection, process hollowing (RunPE), process doppelgänging, atom bombing, hook injection, APC injection, thread execution hijacking, manual mapping, and lesser-known variants using WMI, COM, and ETW consumers.

Detection Analysis

For each technique, Kotler analyzes which API calls are required, which Windows event log entries are generated, and which behavioral patterns can be detected by EDR solutions — providing a practical detection coverage matrix.

Evasion Evolution

The talk traces the adversarial evolution of injection techniques in response to improved detection, showing how each new injection variant was developed specifically to evade the detection mechanisms added for its predecessor.

talks.title: Hila Cohen, Amit Waisel - Malproxy: Leave Your Malware at Home
talks.teaser: Introduces Malproxy, an architecture for executing malicious operations through a reverse proxy that keeps malware off the victim's machine.
talks.summary:
Proxy-Based Malware Architecture

Hila Cohen and Amit Waisel (security researchers, SafeBreach) present Malproxy, a novel attack architecture that separates the malicious payload from the victim's machine by executing it on a remote attacker-controlled server.

Architecture Overview

Malproxy deploys only a thin, seemingly benign agent on the victim machine. The agent establishes a reverse connection to the attacker's server and proxies all system API calls back to the attacker, where the actual malicious code executes in a controlled environment.

Evasion Benefits

Because no malicious code executes on the victim's machine (only the proxy agent), file-based and memory-based malware scanning finds nothing suspicious. AV/EDR products cannot analyze code running on the remote attacker server.

Demonstration

Cohen and Waisel demonstrate running a complete credential dumping operation (LSASS dump) through Malproxy, with only the proxy agent visible on the victim machine and the actual Mimikatz execution occurring on the attacker's server.

talks.title: Joshua Maddux - API Induced SSRF: How ApplePay Scattered Vulns Across the Web
talks.teaser: Discovers widespread SSRF vulnerabilities introduced by Apple Pay merchant validation requirements in e-commerce applications.
talks.summary:
Apple Pay API Induced SSRF

Joshua Maddux (security researcher) presents research identifying a class of SSRF vulnerabilities systematically introduced across thousands of e-commerce sites by Apple Pay integration requirements.

Apple Pay Merchant Validation

Apple Pay requires merchants to validate their identity with Apple's servers during payment sessions via a server-to-server API call. Merchant implementations accept the Apple payment session URL from the client-side JavaScript and proxy the validation request through their own server.

SSRF Introduction Pattern

When merchants implement this validation without validating the provided URL, the endpoint becomes a generic URL-fetching proxy — a textbook SSRF vulnerability. The bug exists in Apple's own integration documentation examples and in third-party payment libraries.

Scope of Impact

Maddux discovers this pattern across hundreds of major e-commerce sites, payment gateways, and SaaS platforms that followed Apple's integration documentation, demonstrating how a single API design decision propagated a vulnerability class at scale across the web ecosystem.

talks.title: Pedro Cabrera Camara - SDR Against Smart TVs: URL Channel Injection Attacks
talks.teaser: Demonstrates injecting malicious DVB-T broadcast signals to attack Smart TVs using commodity SDR hardware.
talks.summary:
Smart TV DVB-T Injection Attacks

Pedro Cabrera Camara presents research on attacking Smart TVs through injected DVB-T (Digital Video Broadcasting – Terrestrial) broadcast signals using commodity software-defined radio hardware.

DVB-T Attack Surface

Digital terrestrial television (DVB-T) uses broadcast frequencies receivable by any antenna. Smart TVs with built-in tuners receive and render HbbTV (Hybrid Broadcast Broadband TV) applications embedded in broadcast streams — web-like applications running in the TV's browser sandbox.

Malicious Broadcast Signal Injection

Using a GNU Radio flow graph and an HackRF SDR transmitter, Camara injects a malicious DVB-T signal stronger than the legitimate broadcast, causing nearby TVs to tune to the injected channel. The injected HbbTV application exploits vulnerabilities in the TV's embedded browser.

Attack Outcomes

Successful exploitation enables loading malicious web content, extracting stored credentials from the TV's browser, pivoting to home network devices via the TV's network interface, and installing persistent malware in the Smart TV's writable storage.

talks.title: phar - No Mas: How Side Channel Flaw Opens ATM, Pharmacies, and Gov to Attack
talks.teaser: Demonstrates timing side-channel attacks against ATM PIN pads, pharmacy dispensing systems, and government ID verification terminals.
talks.summary:
Timing Side Channels in Physical Infrastructure

phar presents timing side-channel vulnerabilities discovered in physical security infrastructure — ATM PIN pads, automated pharmacy dispensing systems, and government ID verification kiosks.

The Timing Oracle

In each target system, cryptographic operations (PIN verification, prescription authorization, identity validation) exhibit measurable timing differences based on whether partial PIN/credential bytes match, enabling byte-by-byte brute force through a timing oracle.

ATM PIN Pad Timing Leak

The PIN verification process in vulnerable ATM firmware leaks timing information proportional to the number of correct prefix bytes, reducing a 4-digit PIN brute force from 10,000 attempts to approximately 40 measurements — making physical PIN capture practical without skimmers.

Pharmacy Dispensing System

Automated pharmacy dispensing systems verify prescription pickup using a 4-digit authorization code with the same timing oracle vulnerability, enabling unauthorized medication access through a timing-based brute force attack.

talks.title: Philippe Laulheret - Intro to Hardware Hacking
talks.teaser: A practical beginner's guide to hardware hacking fundamentals: identifying and exploiting UART, JTAG, and SPI debug interfaces on consumer electronics.
talks.summary:
Hardware Hacking Fundamentals

Philippe Laulheret (Security Researcher, McAfee ATR) delivers a comprehensive practical introduction to hardware security research targeting consumer IoT devices.

Tooling Setup

The talk covers essential hardware hacking tools: multimeters, oscilloscopes, soldering stations, logic analyzers, bus pirate/FT232H adapters, and software (sigrok/PulseView for protocol decoding).

Identifying Debug Interfaces

Laulheret demonstrates techniques for identifying unpopulated UART, JTAG, SWD, and SPI headers on PCBs using visual inspection, continuity testing, and logic analyzer probing. UART ports typically provide Linux shell access at boot time.

Firmware Extraction

The talk covers multiple firmware extraction paths: UART console commands, JTAG memory dumps, SPI flash chip-off using dedicated programmer hardware (FlashCAT, CH341A), and OTA update capture via network interception. Each path is demonstrated against real target devices.

talks.title: Roger Dingledine - The Tor Censorship Arms Race: The Next Chapter
talks.teaser: Tor Project co-founder presents the ongoing arms race between Tor's traffic obfuscation and state-level deep packet inspection censorship systems.
talks.summary:
Tor Censorship Arms Race

Roger Dingledine, co-founder and research director of the Tor Project, presents the ongoing technical arms race between Tor's traffic obfuscation techniques and state-level DPI-based censorship in China, Russia, Iran, and Belarus.

Current Censorship Landscape

National censorship infrastructure (GFW, SORM, IRGC filtering) has become sophisticated at identifying and blocking Tor traffic using deep packet inspection, flow correlation, and active probing. Standard Tor connections are blocked in multiple countries within hours of becoming operational.

Pluggable Transport Evolution

Dingledine traces the development of pluggable transports: obfs3, obfs4, ScrambleSuit, meek (domain fronting), Snowflake (WebRTC-based), and Conjure — each designed to evade the specific detection mechanism used against its predecessor.

Decentralized Bridge Distribution

The current challenge is distributing unlisted Tor bridge addresses to censored users without those addresses being harvested by censors. The talk covers the BridgeDB distribution system, Moat (reCAPTCHA-gated bridge distribution), and Tor's collaboration with major tech companies to provide meek domain fronting.

talks.title: Sheila Ayelen Berta - Backdooring Hardware by Injecting Malicious Payloads on Microcontrollers
talks.teaser: Demonstrates implanting undetectable backdoors in commercial microcontrollers by injecting malicious firmware payloads during the manufacturing process.
talks.summary:
Hardware Backdoor Injection

Sheila Ayelen Berta (Security Researcher, ElevenPaths) presents research on hardware supply chain attacks: injecting malicious firmware payloads into commercial microcontrollers (ATmega, STM32, ESP32) without leaving physical evidence.

Microcontroller Programming Attack Surface

Microcontrollers are typically programmed via ISP (In-System Programming), JTAG, or SWD interfaces. During manufacturing, production programming stations connect to these interfaces to flash device firmware. A compromised programming station could inject additional code alongside the legitimate firmware.

Covert Payload Injection

Berta demonstrates techniques for appending malicious code to existing firmware images while preserving the original functionality — the device operates exactly as expected while executing backdoor functions. The injected code occupies unused flash sections and modifies interrupt vectors.

Detection Evasion

Since the device responds normally to functional tests and the backdoor code is not triggered by standard QA procedures, injected hardware backdoors survive the entire manufacturing quality assurance process. Binary comparison of the device's flash against the reference firmware image is required to detect the modification.

talks.title: smea - Adventures In Smart Buttplug Penetration Testing
talks.teaser: A thorough security analysis of internet-connected intimate devices revealing Bluetooth vulnerabilities, insecure APIs, and privacy failures.
talks.summary:
Security Research: Connected Intimate Devices

smea (security researcher, known for Nintendo 3DS research) presents comprehensive security research on Bluetooth-connected intimate devices — an underexamined IoT category with unique privacy sensitivity.

Device Architecture Analysis

The research covers multiple popular devices from major manufacturers, analyzing their Bluetooth LE protocol implementations, companion mobile applications, and cloud connectivity features. All devices are disassembled for hardware analysis and firmware extraction.

Bluetooth Vulnerabilities

Critical findings include: unauthenticated BLE connections allowing any nearby device to take control, replay attacks that bypass authentication challenges, and trivial brute-force of 4-digit numeric pairing codes across all tested devices.

Privacy and Security Implications

Companion apps transmit usage telemetry, session duration logs, and device control events to cloud servers without user notice. smea demonstrates capturing this data through MitM interception, revealing detailed intimate behavior patterns. The talk advocates for significantly stronger privacy standards in this device category.

talks.title: Stephan Huber - I'm on Your Phone Listening: Attacking VoIP Configuration Interfaces
talks.teaser: Discovers critical authentication bypass and remote code execution vulnerabilities in VoIP phone management interfaces enabling remote eavesdropping.
talks.summary:
VoIP Phone Security Vulnerabilities

Stephan Huber (Security Researcher, Telekom Security) presents research on enterprise VoIP phone security, discovering critical vulnerabilities in the web management interfaces of major VoIP phone manufacturers.

VoIP Phone Attack Surface

Enterprise VoIP phones run embedded Linux with a web management interface for configuration, firmware updates, and diagnostics. These phones sit on corporate networks with access to audio capture capabilities and internal network segments.

Authentication Bypass CVEs

Huber discovers authentication bypass vulnerabilities in the web management interfaces of Grandstream, Yealink, and Snom VoIP phones — allowing unauthenticated access to configuration pages, SIP credential exports, and diagnostic functions.

Remote Eavesdropping

After authentication bypass, the attacker can activate the phone's speakerphone microphone remotely, capture and exfiltrate all audio in the phone's vicinity, and intercept VoIP call audio — turning every corporate conference room phone into a remote listening device.

talks.title: NOC - Everything You Wanted to Know About the DEF CON NOC
talks.teaser: The DEF CON NOC team reveals how they build, operate, and defend the world's most dangerous network for 30,000+ attendees.
talks.summary:
DEF CON Network Operations Center

Neil Wyler (grifter) and Bart Stump present the behind-the-scenes operations of the DEF CON Network Operations Center — the team responsible for designing, deploying, and operating the conference network infrastructure.

Network Architecture

The DC27 network connected 30,000+ conference attendees through a custom-built infrastructure including 40Gbps uplink capacity, wired and wireless access across multiple venues, a dedicated security monitoring layer, and isolated village networks.

Real-Time Attack Response

The NOC operates as both network provider and defensive security team, monitoring for attacks on the network infrastructure, conference systems, and attendee devices in real time. The team responds to dozens of active attack attempts during each conference day.

Notable Incidents

The talk reveals notable incidents observed during DC27: active exploitation of attendee devices on open Wi-Fi, attempted attacks on conference registration systems, and creative attacks on the NOC's own monitoring infrastructure by attendees.

talks.title: Senator Ron Wyden - Can You Track Me Now?
talks.teaser: Senator Ron Wyden presents his legislative efforts to stop US carriers from selling Americans' real-time location data to data brokers.
talks.summary:
Legislative Action on Location Data Surveillance

Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), a member of the Senate Intelligence Committee and longtime digital privacy advocate, presents at DEF CON to discuss his legislative efforts to stop US telecom carriers from selling Americans' real-time location data.

The Location Data Crisis

Following Joseph Cox's Motherboard reporting demonstrating that any American's real-time phone location could be purchased for ~$300 through carrier location data aggregators, Wyden escalated legislative and investigative pressure on the FCC and telecom carriers.

Legislative Proposals

Wyden presents the Mind Your Own Business Act — proposed legislation creating criminal penalties for tech company executives who knowingly mislead the FCC about privacy practices — and the Fourth Amendment is Not for Sale Act, requiring law enforcement to obtain warrants before purchasing location data from data brokers.

FCC Accountability

The senator criticizes FCC Chairman Ajit Pai's failure to act on location data abuses despite extensive documentation, calling for aggressive FCC enforcement action under existing law. Wyden reveals correspondence demanding carrier commitments to cease location data sales.

talks.title: Wenxiang Qian - Breaking Google Home: Exploit it with SQLite
talks.teaser: Achieves remote code execution on Google Home smart speakers by chaining SQLite injection with a use-after-free memory corruption vulnerability.
talks.summary:
Google Home SQLite Exploitation

Wenxiang Qian (Security Researcher, Tencent Blade Team) presents a complete exploit chain for achieving remote code execution on Google Home smart speakers through SQLite vulnerabilities.

Attack Vector: Local Network SQLite Injection

Google Home exposes a local REST API for device discovery and setup. A SQLite database stores device configuration. Qian identifies a SQL injection vulnerability in a specific API endpoint that allows injecting arbitrary SQLite queries.

SQLite as an Exploitation Primitive

Exploiting a SQLite vulnerability for code execution is unconventional. Qian demonstrates using SQLite's LOAD_EXTENSION feature to load arbitrary shared libraries, and uses a UAF (use-after-free) vulnerability in SQLite's virtual table implementation as a memory corruption primitive for ASLR bypass and shell execution.

Full Chain and Impact

The complete exploit chain achieves root shell access on the Google Home from the local network — allowing persistent access to the always-listening microphone, home network traffic interception, and lateral movement to other Google-connected devices.

talks.title: xBen Benmap Morris - Finding Secrets in Publicly Exposed EBS Volumes
talks.teaser: Reveals thousands of publicly exposed AWS EBS snapshots containing plaintext credentials, encryption keys, and production database dumps.
talks.summary:
AWS EBS Snapshot Data Exposure

Ben Morris (security researcher) presents research revealing thousands of publicly exposed Amazon Web Services EBS (Elastic Block Store) snapshots containing sensitive data from production environments.

EBS Snapshot Exposure Mechanism

AWS allows EBS snapshots to be shared publicly for legitimate use cases (distributing AMI base images). Misconfigured AWS accounts accidentally make production volume snapshots public, exposing complete disk images of running EC2 instances.

Automated Discovery at Scale

Morris builds automated tooling that enumerates publicly accessible EBS snapshots by region, mounts them read-only, and scans for sensitive data patterns: passwords, API keys, private keys, database credentials, and PII.

Findings

The research discovers: hundreds of plaintext database dumps with customer PII, thousands of SSH private keys and API credentials for major cloud services, complete source code repositories with embedded secrets, and several Fortune 500 company production configurations — all publicly accessible without any authentication.

talks.title: Xiangqian Zhang - Bugfinding & Exploit Techniques in Android File Transfer Apps
talks.teaser: Discovers multiple critical vulnerabilities in popular Android Wi-Fi file transfer apps through automated fuzzing and manual code review.
talks.summary:
Android File Transfer App Vulnerabilities

Xiangqian Zhang presents research discovering critical vulnerabilities in popular Android file transfer applications used by hundreds of millions of users — apps that create local Wi-Fi servers for cross-device file sharing.

Target Application Category

Apps like Xender, SHAREit, and AirDroid create local HTTP/FTP servers on the Android device's Wi-Fi interface to enable cross-device file transfers. These applications typically run with broad file system permissions to access all device storage.

Vulnerability Discovery

Combining automated fuzzing of the HTTP server component with manual code review, Zhang discovers: unauthenticated arbitrary file read (exposing all device storage), path traversal in upload endpoints enabling arbitrary file write, and code execution via malicious APK delivery through the transfer channel.

Exploit Chains

Zhang demonstrates a complete attack chain from a malicious Wi-Fi hotspot: victim connects to the AP, attacker exploits the file transfer server to install a malicious APK silently, achieving full device compromise against apps with hundreds of millions of installs.

talks.title: XiaoHuiHui - All the 4G Modules Could Be Hacked
talks.teaser: Discovers systemic vulnerabilities across 4G LTE modem modules from major manufacturers used in billions of IoT devices.
talks.summary:
4G Module Vulnerability Research

XiaoHuiHui (security researcher, 360 IoT Security Research Lab) presents research discovering systemic security vulnerabilities across multiple 4G LTE modem modules from major manufacturers — Qualcomm, Quectel, SIMCom, and Sierra Wireless — embedded in billions of IoT devices.

Attack Surface Analysis

4G modules expose multiple interfaces: AT commands over UART/USB, embedded web management pages, and carrier-specific OTA update mechanisms. The modules typically run embedded Linux with the modem firmware, with full network connectivity to the cellular network.

Vulnerabilities Across Vendors

Research reveals common vulnerability classes across all tested vendors: command injection via AT command interfaces, unauthenticated web management interfaces accessible from the cellular network, and OTA update mechanisms without cryptographic signature verification.

Impact Scope

The affected modules power industrial IoT deployments (smart meters, fleet tracking, industrial sensors), connected vehicles (OBD-II adapters, infotainment), medical devices, and smart infrastructure. Exploiting carrier-accessible vulnerabilities enables mass compromise of entire device categories without physical access.

talks.title: Xiaolong Bai - HackPac: Hacking Pointer Authentication in iOS User Space
talks.teaser: Demonstrates practical userspace attacks against ARM Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC) deployed in iOS 12 as a CFI mitigation.
talks.summary:
iOS Pointer Authentication Attacks

Xiaolong Bai (Security Researcher, Alibaba) presents HackPac — research demonstrating practical attacks against ARM Pointer Authentication Codes (PAC), Apple's primary control-flow integrity mitigation in iOS 12+.

Pointer Authentication Background

ARM PAC uses cryptographic signatures embedded in the unused high bits of 64-bit pointers, verified before pointer dereference. Forging a valid PAC requires knowledge of a secret key stored in system registers, preventing ROP/JOP attacks by invalidating gadget chains that use unsigned pointers.

Userspace PAC Bypass Techniques

Bai demonstrates that PAC deployment in iOS userspace contains implementation weaknesses: many library functions sign and verify pointers using context values (discriminators) that are attacker-controllable, enabling PAC forgery without knowledge of the secret key.

Exploit Chain Demonstration

The research demonstrates a complete iOS 12 userspace PAC bypass that chains several weaknesses to forge valid PACs for arbitrary pointers, building a functional ROP chain despite PAC enforcement — enabling code execution from a memory corruption primitive.

talks.title: Xiling Gong - Exploiting Qualcomm WLAN and Modem Over the Air
talks.teaser: Achieves over-the-air code execution on Android phones by exploiting vulnerabilities in Qualcomm WLAN and modem baseband firmware.
talks.summary:
Qualcomm Baseband Over-the-Air Exploitation

Xiling Gong (Security Researcher, Tencent Blade Team) presents research achieving over-the-air code execution on Android smartphones by exploiting vulnerabilities in Qualcomm WLAN and modem baseband firmware.

Baseband Attack Surface

The Qualcomm modem and WLAN chips run separate firmware operating systems (AMSS/QuRT) isolated from the main Android OS. These components process all wireless protocol data (LTE, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth) and represent a powerful attack surface reachable without any user interaction.

WLAN Vulnerabilities

Gong discovers heap overflow vulnerabilities in the Qualcomm WLAN firmware's 802.11 management frame parser (QCACLD-3.0 driver). By transmitting specially crafted Probe Response frames from a malicious access point, the attacker triggers the overflow in the WLAN chip's firmware.

Modem Protocol Stack Attacks

On the LTE modem side, vulnerabilities in the NAS (Non-Access Stratum) protocol implementation allow a malicious base station to trigger memory corruption in the modem firmware, achieving code execution in the baseband OS with full network hardware access.

talks.title: Omer Gull - SELECT Code Execution FROM Using SQLite
talks.teaser: Demonstrates arbitrary code execution achievable through malicious SQLite queries, requiring only a SQL injection primitive in any SQLite-backed application.
talks.summary:
SQLite Code Execution via SQL Injection

Omer Gull (Security Researcher, Checkpoint Research) presents research demonstrating that arbitrary code execution is achievable through carefully crafted SQL queries against SQLite databases, transforming SQL injection into immediate code execution.

SQLite Virtual Tables as Attack Vector

SQLite's virtual table mechanism allows registering C callback functions that execute when virtual tables are queried. While the built-in virtual tables (FTS, R*Tree) are sandboxed, memory corruption vulnerabilities in these implementations allow escalating SQL injection to memory corruption.

Query Planner Exploitation

Gull identifies vulnerabilities in SQLite's query optimizer (query planner) that are triggered by specific query patterns. A malicious SQL query crafted to trigger these bugs achieves heap corruption within the SQLite process.

Universal Impact

Any application with a SQL injection vulnerability against a SQLite backend is immediately vulnerable to code execution via this technique — iOS apps, Android apps, macOS/iOS OS components (SQLite is deeply embedded in Apple platforms), and any backend application using SQLite.

talks.title: Omer Yair - Exploiting Windows Exploit Mitigation for ROP Exploits
talks.teaser: Ironically weaponizes Windows Control Flow Guard (CFG) internals to construct more reliable ROP exploit chains by abusing CFG's bitmap.
talks.summary:
Weaponizing CFG for ROP

Omer Yair (Security Researcher, Checkpoint Research) presents a paradoxical technique: using Windows Control Flow Guard (CFG), a code-flow integrity mitigation, to improve the reliability of ROP exploit chains.

CFG Background

CFG is a Windows exploit mitigation that maintains a bitmap of valid indirect call targets. Before any indirect call or virtual function dispatch, a CFG check verifies the target address exists in the bitmap, preventing ROP chains that call into arbitrary code locations.

Bitmap as Information Leaker

Yair demonstrates that the CFG bitmap itself is a side-channel: by testing whether specific addresses are marked as valid call targets in the CFG bitmap, attackers can enumerate which code pages are mapped and executable in the process — bypassing ASLR without a memory disclosure vulnerability.

CFG as Gadget Identifier

Furthermore, the CFG bitmap marks all valid indirect call targets — which are precisely the function entry points used as ROP/JOP gadgets. By querying the bitmap, attackers enumerate function locations across ASLR-randomized DLLs, dramatically improving gadget chain reliability.

talks.title: Panel: Hacking Congress — The Enemy of My Enemy is My Friend
talks.teaser: Veteran policy advocates discuss practical strategies for engaging Congress on cybersecurity legislation, including coalition building across political lines.
talks.summary:
Engaging Congress on Cybersecurity

Jeff Moss hosts a policy panel with Tarah Wheeler (cybersecurity fellow, New America), Jake Braun (CEO, Cambridge Global Advisors, former DHS official), and Harley Geiger (Director of Public Policy, Rapid7) on effective strategies for influencing federal cybersecurity policy.

Legislative Environment Analysis

The panel provides a realistic assessment of the current congressional environment: members' limited technical literacy, staff's critical gatekeeping role, and the bipartisan nature of cybersecurity issues that creates unusual coalition opportunities across party lines.

Effective Advocacy Strategies

Panelists share what actually works when engaging Congress: building relationships with staff rather than members, translating technical issues into constituent impact language, leveraging think tanks and policy fellowships (Cybersecurity Policy Fellow programs), and coalition building with unexpected allies (insurance industry, rural broadband advocates).

Hacker Community's Role

The panel argues that hackers have unique credibility in policy discussions that lobbyists lack — technical expertise that can't be dismissed. The key is learning to communicate findings in ways that translate to policy action: specific legal changes, budget line items, and regulatory requirements.

talks.title: Truman Kain - Surveillance Detection Scout: Your Lookout on Autopilot
talks.teaser: Introduces an autonomous drone-based surveillance detection system for identifying fixed surveillance positions around a target location.
talks.summary:
Automated Surveillance Detection

Truman Kain presents Surveillance Detection Scout (SDS), an open-source system using consumer drones for automated physical surveillance detection around a target location.

Surveillance Detection Tradecraft

Professional surveillance detection (SD) is a physical security discipline: systematically observing an area to identify fixed surveillance positions (stationary vehicles with occupants, observers at fixed positions) that may indicate law enforcement, intelligence, or criminal monitoring.

Drone-Based Automation

SDS mounts cameras on a DJI Phantom/Mavic drone and uses computer vision (YOLO object detection, vehicle/person recognition) to automatically survey a geographic area, building a model of fixed positions and tracking movement patterns to identify potential surveillance.

Technical Architecture

The system processes drone video feeds in real time using a ground station GPU, applies background subtraction and object tracking, and flags positions where individuals or vehicles remain stationary for extended periods — alerting the operator to potential surveillance threats.
